name: Jílové u Prahy
label: Jílové Old Town
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Masarykovo náměstí' (4 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Masarykovo náměstí' (way/1547458923): middle (108 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/442259: large area 'Jílové u Prahy' (8122 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Historic gold-mining town centre with the main square and church.

text.description: Jílové u Prahy is a small town about 13 km south of Prague, and its old centre is easy to photograph on foot. The best-known picture is taken on Masarykovo náměstí, a sloping rectangular square. The town hall tower stands on one side and the Gothic church of St. Adalbert (sv. Vojtěch) closes the lower end. Together they make a tidy, postcard-style townscape that fits a phone screen well. The town was founded in the 13th century and its early story is tied to gold mining. Its historic centre is well preserved and protected as an urban monument zone. The town hall began as a fortress, and its tower dates from the 14th century. The church is the oldest building in the town, built in the first half of the 13th century on the site of a wooden church. Scenes from the film Amadeus were shot inside it. For your photos, the slope of the square is your friend. Standing in the southern part of the square lets you look toward the church at the lower end of the slope, and the tower gives you a strong vertical to anchor the frame. Keep the phone level so the buildings do not lean, and give the church a little space around it rather than cutting off the spire. If you have time, there are two other views. The Pepř lookout gives a wide panorama over the town and the Sázava valley beyond. Karlova ulice gives a quieter view down the stream valley over the roofs.
text.geographic_location: The spot is in the historic centre of Jílové u Prahy, on Masarykovo náměstí, the town's main square. The town hall tower and the church of St. Adalbert stand around it.
text.directions_text: Jílové u Prahy lies about 13 km south of Prague, on the Prague–Čerčany railway line. Head for the main square, Masarykovo náměstí, in the middle of the old town. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the square, then switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the tower and church will not both fit. Use 2x or more to pick out the tower or the church spire on its own.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Masarykovo náměstí (southern part of the square, looking toward the church of St. Adalbert (sv. Vojtěch)). The sloping rectangular main square with the town hall tower and the Gothic church at its lower end, the classic townscape of the town. From here you look toward the church of St. Adalbert at the lower end of the sloping square, with the town hall tower around it. The wider town centre lies to the north of this point.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the church up with one of the vertical lines so the buildings stay straight. Let the slope of the square lead the eye down to the church, and keep the town hall tower on one side of the frame. For a different view, try the Pepř lookout for a wide panorama, or Karlova ulice for a quiet view over the roofs. Check both before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the church to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out. If the square is busy, take a short burst or a Live Photo and pick the frame with the fewest people in it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed time is confirmed for this view. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a quieter square, but check how it looks on the day.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space with no ticket needed; if you want to go inside the church or up the Pepř lookout, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and a quieter square.
The church interior and the Pepř lookout may have their own access arrangements, so visitors should check before going.
Keeping the phone level and using gridlines helps keep buildings from appearing to lean.

name: Žampach Viaduct
label: Žampach Viaduct
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/819651314: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Žampašský viadukt' (114 m across).
notes: Historic 1899 stone railway viaduct, best photographed looking up from below.

text.description: The Žampach Viaduct is a seven-arch stone railway bridge that carries the line from Vrané nad Vltavou to Čerčany across a valley near the village of Žampach. It is the highest stone bridge in the Czech Republic, at 41.73 m. It is 109.3 m long, and each of its seven arches is 12 m wide. It was built between 1898 and 1900, mainly by Italian workers, and in 2013 the Czech National Bank put it on a coin. It photographs well because the repeating arches give a strong rhythm, and the pale stone stands out against the trees around it. Your main challenge is fitting it in. Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) and tilt the phone upwards to catch the height of the piers and the line of arches. Then switch to the default lens (1x) or the telephoto (2x-5x) for tighter shots of a single arch or the stonework. Take a few of each, as the viaduct looks quite different close up and from a distance. Stay on public ground and keep well away from the railway itself.
text.geographic_location: The viaduct is in the territory of Jílové u Prahy, beside the village of Žampach. It crosses a valley on the railway line between Luka pod Medníkem and Jílové u Prahy stations.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed close to this spot. The viaduct is near the village of Žampach in the Jílové u Prahy area, so check a map for the way there. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) to fit the full height and the row of arches into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a more natural view, and the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the stonework and single arches.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Stay on public ground and do not walk onto the railway or its embankment.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line them up with the piers, so the verticals look straight rather than leaning. Tilt the phone up gently and leave some space around the top of the structure. For a different view, step back, switch to 1x or the telephoto, and photograph a few arches at a time so the repeating curves fill the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the sky or stone, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not turn white. If your phone has a panorama mode, hold it upright and sweep from bottom to top for a tall shot, keeping the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft, even light on a bright but slightly overcast day suits the stonework best. In strong sun, the shadows under the arches can be very dark, so check your exposure.

text.access_note: The viaduct carries a railway line, so enjoy it from public ground only, never go onto the tracks, and check locally for access before you go.

photo.from: Own photo, taken 3 m from the phone icon

name: St John's Rapids
label: St John's Rapids
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Smetanova vyhlídka' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Smetanova vyhlídka' (node/1659232162): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q12057341: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Famous former rapids of the Vltava river, now flooded by the reservoir.

text.description:
St John's Rapids (Svatojánské proudy) was once a stretch of fast-flowing water on the Vltava. You can no longer see the rapids themselves. The Štěchovice reservoir flooded them in 1943, so what you photograph today is calm water in a deep, wooded river valley. The rapids were part of the inspiration for Smetana's Má vlast, and they also gave their name to an opera by Josef Richard Rozkošný, so the place still matters to Czech music lovers.

One viewpoint over the valley of the former rapids is Smetanova vyhlídka, a terrace near the Ztracenka campsite area. It was built for the 150th anniversary of Smetana's birth, which ties it neatly to the story. It is a quieter alternative to the better-known Vyhlídka Máj, which looks down on the river's horseshoe-shaped bend in the rocky canyon. From the terrace you look out over the valley of the former rapids, so the picture is about the curve of the river, the steep slopes and the sense of depth, not about a single landmark.

A phone suits this well. Keep the horizon level using gridlines, and include some foreground such as the terrace edge or trees to give the valley scale. If you also visit Vyhlídka Máj, take care: it has no railing or platform, and the pasture on the route is fenced with an electric fence. Stay well back from any drop when you take a picture.
text.geographic_location: The viewpoint is on the Vltava valley side near the Ztracenka campsite area, reached by a branch road from Teletín, within the Jílové u Prahy map area. The former rapids lie below, under the Štěchovice reservoir.
text.directions_text: No public transport is listed for this spot. Start from the town of Jílové u Prahy and head towards Teletín. From Teletín, a branch road leads to the Ztracenka campsite area, where Smetanova vyhlídka is. Its position is not precisely pinned down, so check it on the map before you set off. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the valley. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in more of the slopes and sky, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the bend in the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Smetanova vyhlídka (near the Ztracenka campsite area, reached by a branch road from Teletín). A quieter alternative overlooking the river valley of the former rapids; no page gives a detailed description of the framing. Face that way so the river valley fills the frame. The exact position of Smetanova vyhlídka is not confirmed, so check it on the map before relying on it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the far hillside on the upper third line, with the water in the lower part. Include a bit of the terrace edge or nearby trees in the foreground for depth. If you want the horseshoe-shaped bend of the river in the canyon, Vyhlídka Máj is the alternative viewpoint, but there is no railing there, so take care.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the far hillside to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the water and trees keep their colour. Try a panorama, moving the phone slowly, to catch the whole valley.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a wooded valley and the water, and a clear day helps. Midday sun can make the reservoir glare.

text.access_note: Smetanova vyhlídka appears to be an open viewpoint, but confirm its location and access on the map before you go, and take care on the rock at Vyhlídka Máj, which has no railing.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters a wooded valley and the water.
Midday sun can make the reservoir surface glare in photos.
Smetanova vyhlídka appears to be an open viewpoint without an entry fee or restricted access.

name: Kamenný Přívoz
label: Kamenný Přívoz
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Most Kamenný Přívoz' (2 web pages); placed at our map tiles: 'Kamenný přívoz' (pois).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/442233: large area 'Kamenný Přívoz' (4663 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Small village on the Sázava river, popular with hikers and boaters.

text.description:
Kamenný Přívoz is a village on the Sázava River in the Central Bohemian Region, with about 1,600 inhabitants. Its German name is Steinüberfuhr. It is made up of four municipal parts, and the river runs through the middle of the scene. The best phone picture here shows how the village sits in the valley. From the road bridge you look across the Sázava toward the church of St. Ludmila. The bridge is the main link between the two halves of the village, so you stand at the place that ties the view together.

The river gives you a natural leading line, and the church gives the picture a clear point of interest. The view works well as a wide scene of valley, water and rooftops, and also as a closer shot of the church of St. Ludmila.

Before you go, note that the bridge is under reconstruction, with long traffic detours planned until about May 2027. Access and the view from the deck may be restricted, so check on site. If you can stand on the bridge, take care around traffic and check on site whether there is a safe place to stand. If you have time for a longer walk, the Žampažská vyhlídka looks across the river toward the Žampach railway viaduct and down onto the weir. It is a trail walk of about 5 km from Jílové u Prahy, not a quick stop.
text.geographic_location: The village lies on the Sázava River in Prague-West District, and the spot is shown on the Jílové u Prahy map.
text.directions_text: No station, tram stop or other public transport stop is listed for this spot. Head for the road bridge over the Sázava in the village of Kamenný Přívoz. If the bridge is closed or restricted, check on site for the nearest safe place to view the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the river, the bridge and the village together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you want more of the valley and sky. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the church of St. Ludmila across the river.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Most Kamenný Přívoz (from the bridge over the Sázava, looking toward the church side of the village). The Sázava valley and the village, with the church of St. Ludmila visible across the river from the bridge deck. From here you look across the Sázava toward the village, with the church of St. Ludmila on the far side. Face the church side of the village for the main shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the river along a lower third line, so the water leads the eye toward the church. Keep any bridge railing low or out of the frame, or use it as a soft foreground edge. For a second picture, zoom in on the church of St. Ludmila. If you walk to the Žampažská vyhlídka, you can try a different shot across the river toward the railway viaduct and the weir.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the church or the far bank to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright so it keeps its colour. Hold the phone steady against something solid, or against your body, for the zoomed shot. Take a few frames, since traffic may shake the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually flatters the water and the village, but check the light on the day. The bridge works can change what you can do, so look at the situation when you arrive.

text.access_note: The bridge is a public road bridge but is under reconstruction until about May 2027, so access and the view from the deck may be restricted; check on site before you go.
